mcqs.question: The `satisfied` counter in the need-map pattern changes by exactly one precisely when what happens?
options: The entire window map is compared against the entire need map
Any character at all is added to or removed from the window, whether or not it appears in need
The window is re-checked for validity on a fixed schedule of steps
A specific character's count in the window crosses its required threshold in need, in either direction
mcqs.explanation: satisfied is designed to update in O(1) exactly at the moment a character's count in the window passes its need threshold, up or down — that's what makes overall validity an O(1) check instead of an O(distinct characters) scan. Characters not in need never touch it, and there's no fixed schedule involved.

mcqs.question: In Minimum Window Substring, why does the code check `window[c] == need[c]` (equality) rather than `window[c] >= need[c]` when deciding whether to increment satisfied?
options: Equality is used purely for style; >= would behave identically here
Because a character's count only ever increases during expansion, so checking >= would re-trigger the increment every time the count exceeds the threshold again on later duplicates
Because using >= would raise a KeyError whenever c isn't a key in need
Because every value in need is guaranteed to equal exactly 1 in this problem
mcqs.explanation: satisfied should increment exactly once, the moment a character first reaches its requirement — using >= without an equality check would fire again on every subsequent duplicate of that character, double-counting satisfaction and corrupting the running total. need[c] is not restricted to 1, and the KeyError concern is handled separately by the `c in need` guard.

mcqs.question: Checking window validity with a full map comparison every step, instead of maintaining a satisfied counter, has what actual consequence?
options: It produces a wrong count of matching windows
It raises an immediate runtime error on any input longer than the target
The algorithm's time complexity gains a dependency on the target's distinct character count k, turning O(n) into O(n·k)
It has no measurable effect; both approaches have identical asymptotic complexity
mcqs.explanation: Both approaches give the same correct answer — the full-comparison version just pays an extra O(k) cost on every single step to re-derive what the satisfied counter tracks incrementally, which only shows up as a real problem once k or n gets large. No exception is raised, and the output itself is identical, just slower.

mcqs.question: In Permutation in String, why must the outgoing character's satisfied check happen before decrementing its window count, not after?
options: Because decrementing first would raise a KeyError for that character
Because Python dictionaries don't allow decrementing a value in place
It doesn't actually matter which order these two operations happen in
The check needs the count while it still reflects whether the character was exactly meeting its requirement — decrementing first would compare against an already-changed value
mcqs.explanation: satisfied should only decrease if removing this character actually drops it below its required threshold — checking after decrementing would evaluate the wrong (already-reduced) count and could misjudge the transition. There's no dictionary limitation involved, and swapping the order silently miscounts satisfied rather than crashing.

mcqs.question: A palindrome-rearrangement problem needs to track whether each character's count is odd or even rather than its exact count. What actually changes in the need-map pattern?
options: Nothing — the exact-count comparison logic in the counter update applies completely unchanged
The whole pattern becomes inapplicable and a different technique entirely is required
What the map stores and what crossing a threshold means — parity flips instead of raw counts — while the underlying mechanics of an incrementally maintained O(1) summary stay the same
The window must be re-sorted after every single character is added or removed
mcqs.explanation: The reusable idea is maintaining some O(1) summary of the window incrementally rather than rescanning it — what that summary tracks (exact counts, parities, category coverage) is the part that changes per problem, not the discipline of updating it in O(1) on each edit. Sorting has no role in either the original or the parity-based variant.
